Question: In today's pandemic crisis, how does one come up with a value for human life in the cost-benefit analysis?
Answer: I think that a major flaw that is being used by many with today’s pandemic crisis is trying to place a monetary value on lives saved from COVID-19 in the cost benefit-analysis. Instead of considering how just how many lives might be saved from measures taken to combat COVID-19, it should also be calculated how many lives will be lost due to the same measures. One thing that I have learned in life, is that there is no free lunch. Someone always has to pay for the lunch, and many times the person receiving the lunch finds out later that they have a debt accruing for that “free” lunch. Here is an example of the common way of doing cost benefit analysis on lives versus money: Social Distancing: Are The Costs Of Shutting Down The Economy Worth It? Here are two articles that outlines some of the potential domestic health threats of the economy shutdown: What a Prolonged Shutdown Will Cost in Human Life | RealClearPolitics How Shutting Down The Economy Could Kill Tens Of Thousands Now in a worldwide perspective, the UN and other international organizations have been communicating the distinct possibility that a collective effect of the shut down of economies could put hundreds of millions of people around the world on the edge of starvation: U.N. warns 'hunger pandemic' looming amid fight against coronavirus For sure estimating the potential loss of life due to government restrictions put in place to fight COVID-19 is a complex task. Regardless it needs to be attempted. That way we can find a balance point where the least total lives will be lost. We should also evaluate many of the restrictions as to how many lives if any they are likely to save. For example, 20 kids playing a sandlot game of baseball, preventing this will save how many lives? And can we go from government restrictions, to government recommendations and letting people govern themselves without significant loss of life. Many believe that we can do so, such as Sweden has done, without adding additional long term loss of life to COVID-19. Finally, I think that there needs to be a measured cost in lives saved versus precedents for doing away with rights such as right to assemble, right to worship as you choose, and many more. There have been extremely violent confrontations between law enforcement and citizens protesting for their rights. Is this helping more than hurting? How much of our rights should be given up for additional safety? Or should we give up any rights at all? All these questions should be factored in. And not all can be or should be answered by experts. I and my wife are in the very high risk category for COVID-19. I have a laundry list of serious and chronic illnesses including two serious chronic respiratory conditions. We plan to limit our contact with the outside world as much as possible and take all reasonable precautions. I don’t need the government to try and force me to do this, and if I put myself at risk and contact COVID-19 then I will likely suffer the consequences. But my neighbors are relatively young and healthy, why should they be forced to take the same precautions as me? Does making my neighbors take these precautions really make me and other high risk people more vulnerable? Or does forcing precautions on low risk people delay herd immunity and put me at more not less risk? I don’t pretend to have all or even most of the answers to these questions. But I think much more thought and analysis needs to go into deciding government action than lives saved from COVID-19 vs money lost from economy. Question: Is Bill Russell overrated because of the era he played in? Can he dominate in any era?
Answer: Is Bill Russell overrated because of the era he played in? Can he dominate in any era? Bill Russell was a dominant player who is generally overrated in how dominant he was because of special aspects of the era that Russell played in. This doesn’t mean that Russell could not have been a dominant player in most if not all eras. It does mean that he most likely would have been less dominant in most other NBA eras. How was Russell overrated? Well Russell is listed as the player with the most NBA championship rings with 11 total. The only player that comes close to that is Sam Jones who was Russell’s teammate for 10 out of those 11 championships. Of the players that have 7 or more championship rings all of them are either Bill Russell or teammates of Bill Russell when winning their rings except for Rober Horry who won rings as a role player for 3 different NBA franchises with either Shaquille O’Neil, Hakeem Olajuwon, or Time Duncan as teammates. If you look at players who won 6 or more championships you’ll find Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen who won 6 as teammates of each other, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar who won 5 as Magic Johnson’s teammate and 1 as Oscar Robertson’s teammate, and then Bob Cousy who won 6 as Bill Russell’s teammate. What does all that tell us? Well it tells us that Bill Russell had a lot of help from a lot of All-Time great players to win his championships. While no player won as many championships as Russell did, no player was remotely close to having as much help as Russell did either. Russell was a key player in all 11 championships, but there were many other players at least of similar importance in winning those championships. Russell never won a single championship where he was the only All-Star on the team. Several players have won a championship where they were the only All-Star on their team. Bill Russell is also known as individually being one of the best rebounders in NBA history. Russell is 2nd All-Time in rebounds per game in the regular season and 1st All-Time in rebounds per game in the playoffs. But this overrates Russell’s rebound ability slightly because Russell had some factors in his era that allowed for him to having a higher rate of rebounds than players in other eras. Part of this was Russell played in an era with a pace much higher than other eras by 20 to 30%. Part was Russell played in the era where there were the most total rebounds to be grabbed per game. It you looke at the percent of rebounds that Russell grabbed vs the percent that other players grabbed such as Dennis Rodman or Moses Malone, you’ll find percentagewise Russell is not quite as good but in rebounds per game he is better. This means Russell would likely have done well in Dennis Rodman’s era, but maybe not as good as Dennis did. So in conclusion, please be sure to give Bill Russell credit as being an All-Time NBA great player. But also temper that credit slightly due to some advantages that Russell had because of the style and quality of play in his era or due to the overabundance of quality teammates compared to 99.999% of other players.

Question: What are some remarkable moments on the court where Michael Jordan made mistakes showing he is, in the end, human?
Answer: What are some remarkable moments on the court where Michael Jordan made mistakes showing he is, in the end, human? What’s something that is human? Well losing a playoff series when your team has homecourt advantage is something all superstar players that I’ve ever heard of have done at one point in time or another. The list is long: Lebron, Wilt, Bill Russell, Kareem, Hakeem, Step, Jokic, Kevin Durrant, Magic, Bird, Jerry West, Elgin Baylor, Oscar Robinson, Dr J, Tim Duncan, Kobe, Isaiah, and Shaq to name a few superstars who lost a playoff series when having homecourt advantage. OK let’s review all the times Jordan lost in the playoffs when his Bulls held homecourt advantage in a playoff series and ended up losing the playoff series. Oh, seems like Jordan played in 24 playoff series where his team, the Bulls, had homecourt advantage and they won all 24 series. In fact, the Bulls only faced a total of 3 elimination games when having homecourt advantage, a single time in 3 playoff series: 1998 ECF vs Indiana Pacers, 1992 EC 2nd rounds against the NY Knicks, and 1988 EC 1st round against the Cleveland Cavaliers. None of the elimination games was decided by less than 5 points. … OK, but how about all those playoff series where Jordan wasn’t the top scorer for his team? I mean all the other great scorers in NBA history have had off series where they weren’t playing at the top of the NBA and certainly had several series where they weren’t the top scorer. OK let’s find and analyse all the playoff series where Jordan wasn’t the top scorer for his team. Er, there don’t seem to be any playoff series where Jordan wasn’t the top scorer for his team. Even worse, of the 37 playoff series that Jordan played in, he was the top scorer 36 times. Only 1 time did another player on either team score more points than Jordan. That happened in Jordan’s 1st playoff series against the Milwaukee Bucks where Jordan’s Bulls took on a team that had 21 more regular season wins than they did (59 to 38), more All-NBA players (2 to 1 [Jordan]), more 1st team All-Defense players (2 to 0), and who had the 2nd rated defense in the NBA as well as the 2nd rated NET rating in the NBA. The Bulls won 1 of 4 games while Jordan was outscored by All-NBA 2nd teammer Terry Cummings 118 points to Jordan’s 117 points. Jordan led all players with 8.5 assists per game, 2 more assists per game than the next closest player Paul Pressy of the Bucks. Overall Jordan performed a “choke job” against the Bucks by leading all NBA players in the 1985 playoffs in 5 categories: Minutes per game, steals per game, PER, OBPM, and BPM. Any rookie should be ashamed to show their face after ONLY leading all NBA players JUST 5 categories. 🙄🙄🙄🙄🙄 … Yeah, but what about all those long losing streaks that the Bulls went on during Jordan’s peak years? Every major superstar has had times during their peak years where they’ve gone on several game losing streaks and had to find a way to pull themselves out of it. Generally, an NBA player’s peak years are considered to be between ages 28 to 34. Let’s take a look at the long losing streaks that the Bulls had during Jordan’s peak years. Well, it seems like in Jordan’s peak years, the Bulls never lost more than 2 games in a row while Michael Jordan was on the roster. The Bulls lost the 1st 3 games of the 1990–1991 season and never lost 3 in a row again while Jordan was on the playoff roster including regular season and playoff games. I know of no other NBA superstar that can make this claim. Now this doesn’t include the 147 regular season games and 10 playoff games Jordan was retired for between November 5th, 1993 to March 18th, 1995. It does include the 6 regular season games he missed during the 1991–1992 and 1993 and 1994 seasons.

Question: Why did LeBron James reach the NBA Finals before Michael Jordan did?
Answer: Why did LeBron James reach the NBA Finals before Michael Jordan did? Essentially the question boils down to why was Lebron able to lead his team to advance to finals earlier in his career than when Jordan was able to lead his team to advance to the finals. I pondered this and was in the midst of writing a long and complex answer when I realized the answer was far more simple than I was making it. Lebron was able to do this because he was presented with an easier opportunity to do so that Jordan had until Jordan’s 7th season. Let’s boil it down as to exactly what happened when the Cavs advanced to the Finals in 2007 by beating two 41 win teams and a 53 win Pistons team. In Lebron’s first 7 seasons in Cleveland, his Cavs never beat a 50+ win team other than the Pistons. Now in Jordan’s 1st six seasons his Bulls were eliminated by teams than won more than 53 games. 54 wins > 53 Wins, so MJ never had as good a chance to advance as Lebron did in 2007.
